claim: Channelrhodopsins (ChRs) are microbial light-gated ion channels utilized in optogenetics to control neural activity with light.
source: Channelrhodopsins (ChRs) are microbial light-gated ion channels utilized in optogenetics to control neural activity with light .
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation marker in the manuscript.

claim: Light absorption causes retinal chromophore isomerization and subsequent protein conformational changes visualized as optically distinguished intermediates, coupled with channel opening and closing.
source: Light absorption causes retinal chromophore isomerization and subsequent protein conformational changes visualized as optically distinguished intermediates, coupled with channel opening and closing.
evidence: This is a general description of the photocycle process in channelrhodopsins, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The detailed molecular events underlying channel gating remain unknown.
source: However, the detailed molecular events underlying channel gating remain unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Time-resolved serial femtosecond crystallographic analyses of ChR using an X-ray free electron laser revealed conformational changes following photoactivation.
source: We performed time-resolved serial femtosecond crystallographic analyses of ChR by using an X-ray free electron laser, which revealed conformational changes following photoactivation.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding of the study, supported by the TR-SFX data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The isomerized retinal adopts a twisted conformation and shifts toward the putative internal proton donor residues.
source: The isomerized retinal adopts a twisted conformation and shifts toward the putative internal proton donor residues, consequently inducing an outward shift of TM3, as well as a local deformation in TM7.
evidence: This is supported by the difference Fourier maps and structural refinement data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The isomerized retinal induces an outward shift of TM3.
source: The isomerized retinal adopts a twisted conformation and shifts toward the putative internal proton donor residues, consequently inducing an outward shift of TM3, as well as a local deformation in TM7.
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps shown in Figure 4.

claim: The isomerized retinal induces a local deformation in TM7.
source: The isomerized retinal adopts a twisted conformation and shifts toward the putative internal proton donor residues, consequently inducing an outward shift of TM3, as well as a local deformation in TM7.
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps shown in Figure 4.

claim: Early conformational changes in the pore-forming helices are the triggers that lead to opening of the ion conducting pore.
source: These early conformational changes in the pore-forming helices should be the triggers that lead to opening of the ion conducting pore.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structural changes and their timing relative to channel opening.

claim: ChRs were first identified as sensory photoreceptors in green algae.
source: Channelrhodopsins (ChRs) are light-gated cation channels first identified as sensory photoreceptors in green algae (Nagel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Nagel et al., 2003.

claim: ChRs consist of seven transmembrane helices and a retinal chromophore covalently attached to a conserved lysine residue via a Schiff base linkage.
source: ChRs consist of seven transmembrane helices and a retinal chromophore covalently attached to a conserved lysine residue via a Schiff base linkage.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about channelrhodopsins.

claim: ChRs allow fast ion flux across cell membranes upon illumination.
source: ChRs allow fast ion flux across cell membranes upon illumination and thus are widely utilized as optogenetic tools to precisely control neural activity (Schneider et al., 2015; Ernst et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Light absorption triggers all-trans to 13-cis isomerization of the retinal in ChRs.
source: As in the well-studied bacterial proton pump bacteriorhodopsin (BR), light absorption triggers all-trans to 13-cis isomerization of the retinal, and induces the transitions of optically distinguishable intermediates that lead to channel opening and closing (photocycle process) (Kuhne et al., 2019; Bamann et al., 2010; Bamann et al., 2008; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and comparison to bacteriorhodopsin.

claim: Retinal isomerization induces transitions of optically distinguishable intermediates that lead to channel opening and closing.
source: As in the well-studied bacterial proton pump bacteriorhodopsin (BR), light absorption triggers all-trans to 13-cis isomerization of the retinal, and induces the transitions of optically distinguishable intermediates that lead to channel opening and closing (photocycle process) (Kuhne et al., 2019; Bamann et al., 2010; Bamann et al., 2008; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a fundamental aspect of the ChR photocycle.

claim: In CrChR2, retinal isomerization leads to an intermediate with a red-shifted absorption peak, P1520.
source: In the best studied variant, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii ChR2 (CrChR2) (Bamann et al., 2008; Stehfest and Hegemann, 2010; Lórenz-Fonfría et al., 2013), retinal isomerization leads to an intermediate with a red-shiftedabsorption peak, P1520 (K or L in BR), and sequential deprotonation and reprotonation of the Schiff base generate P2390 and P3520 (M and N in BR), respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the CrChR2 photocycle.

claim: Sequential deprotonation and reprotonation of the Schiff base generate P2390 and P3520 intermediates in CrChR2.
source: In the best studied variant, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii ChR2 (CrChR2) (Bamann et al., 2008; Stehfest and Hegemann, 2010; Lórenz-Fonfría et al., 2013), retinal isomerization leads to an intermediate with a red-shiftedabsorption peak, P1520 (K or L in BR), and sequential deprotonation and reprotonation of the Schiff base generate P2390 and P3520 (M and N in BR), respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the photocycle intermediates.

claim: Photocycle transitions are determined in most ChRs by an aspartate–cysteine pair in the retinal binding pocket (DC-pair).
source: Photocycle transitions are determined in most ChRs by an aspartate–cysteine pair in the retinal binding pocket (DC-pair) (Berndt et al., 2009; Yizhar et al., 2011; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the mechanism by which ion pore formation is associated with these residues is still under debate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying the DC-pair.

claim: The mechanism by which ion pore formation is associated with the DC-pair residues is still under debate.
source: Photocycle transitions are determined in most ChRs by an aspartate–cysteine pair in the retinal binding pocket (DC-pair) (Berndt et al., 2009; Yizhar et al., 2011; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the mechanism by which ion pore formation is associated with these residues is still under debate.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap regarding the DC-pair mechanism.

claim: The ion conducting pore is formed during the late P2390 intermediate.
source: Recent studies have suggested that the ion conducting pore is formed during the late P2390 intermediate Kuhne et al., 2019, involving the rearrangement of the pore-forming TM helices (Müller et al., 2011), and a two-dimensional crystal study indeed revealed low resolution projection maps of the light-induced helix movement in ChR (Müller et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Ion pore formation involves the rearrangement of the pore-forming TM helices.
source: Recent studies have suggested that the ion conducting pore is formed during the late P2390 intermediate Kuhne et al., 2019, involving the rearrangement of the pore-forming TM helices (Müller et al., 2011), and a two-dimensional crystal study indeed revealed low resolution projection maps of the light-induced helix movement in ChR (Müller et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: A two-dimensional crystal study revealed low resolution projection maps of the light-induced helix movement in ChR.
source: Recent studies have suggested that the ion conducting pore is formed during the late P2390 intermediate Kuhne et al., 2019, involving the rearrangement of the pore-forming TM helices (Müller et al., 2011), and a two-dimensional crystal study indeed revealed low resolution projection maps of the light-induced helix movement in ChR (Müller et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the 2D crystal studies.

claim: C1C2 has normal ChR1 photocycle properties.
source: We used a chimeric construct between Chlamydomonas reinhardtii ChR1 (CrChR1) and ChR2 (CrChR2) for the TR-SFX experiments (hereafter referred to as C1C2) (Kato et al., 2012; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which has normal ChR1 photocycle properties (Hontani et al., 2017; Inaguma et al., 2015; Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous characterization studies.

claim: C1C2 yielded high-density microcrystals that diffracted XFEL to about 2.3 Å at SACLA.
source: C1C2 yielded high-density microcrystals that diffracted XFEL to about 2.3 Å at SACLA (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is directly supported by the diffraction data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The dark state structure of C1C2 determined at SACLA is almost the same as the previous structure solved by the synchrotron analysis.
source: The dark state structure of C1C2 determined at SACLA is almost the same as the previous structure solved by the synchrotron analysis, including the chromophore retinal, the interhelical interactions of the inner and central gates, and the extracellular water access channel in the dark state (Figure 3c,d, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Hontani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with the previous synchrotron structure and shown in Figure 3.

claim: C1C2 showed similar photo-intermediates as observed in the previous study in detergent micelles or reconstituted lipid membranes.
source: In the flash-photolysis experiments, C1C2 showed similar photo-intermediates as observed in the previous study (Hontani et al., 2017), in detergent micelles or reconstituted lipid membranes (Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the flash-photolysis data shown in Figure 2 and comparison to previous studies.

claim: C1C2 shows a rapid rise of 520 nm absorption after photo-excitation, occurring before 10 μs, which corresponds to the formation of the P1 intermediate.
source: The results indicate a rapid rise of 520 nm absorption after photo-excitation, occurring before 10 μs, which corresponds to the formation of the P1 intermediate with an isomerized retinal (Hontani et al., 2017; Nogly et al., 2018), and the subsequent increases at 390 nm and 520 nm show formation of the P2 and P3 intermediates with a deprotonated and reprotonated retinal Schiff base, respectively (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the transient absorption data in Figure 2a and citations.

claim: Subsequent increases at 390 nm and 520 nm show formation of the P2 and P3 intermediates with a deprotonated and reprotonated retinal Schiff base, respectively.
source: The results indicate a rapid rise of 520 nm absorption after photo-excitation, occurring before 10 μs, which corresponds to the formation of the P1 intermediate with an isomerized retinal (Hontani et al., 2017; Nogly et al., 2018), and the subsequent increases at 390 nm and 520 nm show formation of the P2 and P3 intermediates with a deprotonated and reprotonated retinal Schiff base, respectively (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the transient absorption data in Figure 2a.

claim: The delayed rise of the 530 nm absorption after 360 μs shows the formation of the P3 intermediate at the later time point.
source: The absorption spectra of P1 and P3 resemble each other and cannot be distinguished in C1C2, but the delayed rise of the 530 nm absorption after 360 μs shows the formation of the P3 intermediate at the later time point.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-resolved absorption data.

claim: The C1C2 photocurrents are initiated by a fast, inward directed charge transfer that likely coincides with the retinal deprotonation (P2 formation).
source: The C1C2 photocurrents are initiated by a fast, inward directed charge transfer that likely coincides with the retinal deprotonation (P2 formation), which has not been fully time-resolved in the whole cell patch clamp recordings.
evidence: This is supported by the photocurrent measurements shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Passive photocurrents rise with a time constant of 70–140 µs in C1C2.
source: Afterwards, passive photocurrents rise with a time constant of 70–140 µs (rather faster at acidic pH) and change direction depending on the membrane voltage.
evidence: This is directly measured from the photocurrent data.

claim: The photocurrent remains after reprotonation of the retinal Schiff base and declines in a biexponential manner.
source: The photocurrent remains after reprotonation of the retinal Schiff base and declines in a biexponential manner, with two voltage dependent time constants of 8–40 ms and 60–130 ms and a kinetic amplitude ratio that depends on the pH, correlating neither precisley with the P2nor the P3 intermediate.
evidence: This is directly measured from the photocurrent data.

claim: The absorption spectrum of ChR depends mostly on the microenvironment of the chromophore retinal, especially on the Schiff base environment.
source: The absorption spectrum of ChR depends mostly on the microenvironment of the chromophore retinal, especially on the Schiff base environment (Ritter et al., 2008), and does not need to reflect changes in the ion pore structure .
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: C1C2 channel opening takes place only after deprotonation of the retinal Schiff base, during further confirmational changes of the P2 intermediate.
source: As recently shown for CrChR2 (Kuhne et al., 2019), also C1C2 channel opening takes place only after deprotonation of the retinal Schiff base, during further confirmational changes of the P2 intermediate.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to CrChR2 and the photocurrent data.

claim: Flash illumination induced a rapid elevation at 530 nm in C1C2 LCP crystals, confirming retinal isomerization (P1 formation).
source: The flash illumination induced a rapid elevation at 530 nm, confirming retinal isomerization (P1 formation) (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a, c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The elevation of the 390 nm absorption, most prominent in 2.1–21 ms, showed P2 formation in C1C2 crystals.
source: The elevation of the 390 nm absorption, which is most prominent in 2.1–21 ms, showed the P2 formation, but the subsequent increase at the 530 nm absorption was not observed in the crystal (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a,c), suggesting that the transition from P2 to P3 is hindered in the crystal, although the C1C2 crystal has only minimal interactions at the extracellular membrane region (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal spectroscopy data.

claim: The transition from P2 to P3 is hindered in the C1C2 crystal.
source: The elevation of the 390 nm absorption, which is most prominent in 2.1–21 ms, showed the P2 formation, but the subsequent increase at the 530 nm absorption was not observed in the crystal (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a,c), suggesting that the transition from P2 to P3 is hindered in the crystal, although the C1C2 crystal has only minimal interactions at the extracellular membrane region (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of the P3 signature in the crystal spectroscopy data.

claim: The accumulation of the P2 intermediate is more prominent in the crystals compared to micelles and reconstituted membranes.
source: Nonetheless, the accumulation of the P2 intermediate is more prominent in the crystals, as the spectral increase at 390 nm is relatively higher, as compared to the similar increase detected in micelles and reconstituted membranes (Figure 2a,d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 3b,d).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the spectroscopy data from crystals and solution.

claim: The flash photo-activation experiment using HEK cells showed that the photocurrent rose in between 100–1000 μs, regardless of pH.
source: In addition, the flash photo-activation experiment using HEK cells showed that the photocurrent rose in between 100–1000 μs, regardless of pH, which corresponds to a second late P2 intermediate (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in a good agreement with the previous studies in ChR2 (Kuhne et al., 2015; Kuhne et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly measured from the photocurrent data in HEK cells.

claim: The photocurrent rise between 100–1000 μs corresponds to a second late P2 intermediate.
source: In addition, the flash photo-activation experiment using HEK cells showed that the photocurrent rose in between 100–1000 μs, regardless of pH, which corresponds to a second late P2 intermediate (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in a good agreement with the previous studies in ChR2 (Kuhne et al., 2015; Kuhne et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of photocurrent rise and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The difference-Fourier maps clearly revealed the structural changes in the protein core region of C1C2.
source: The difference-Fourier maps were calculated at 2.5 Å for each delayed time point, with the dark state SFX structure as the reference (Figure 4), and they clearly revealed the structural changes in the protein core region of C1C2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Video 1).
evidence: This is directly shown in the difference Fourier maps in Figure 4.

claim: The quantum efficiency of the retinal isomerization is estimated as only about 30% in C1C2.
source: Due to the low quantum efficiency of the retinal isomerization, which is estimated as only about 30% in C1C2 (Hontani et al., 2017), we calculated the extrapolated structure factor amplitudes and the models were refined against the extrapolated maps (detailed in Materials and methods and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The isomerization of the retinal induces conformational changes of the retinal-linked residue, Lys296, and TM7.
source: The isomerization of the retinal induces conformational changes of the retinal-linked residue, Lys296, and TM7 (Figure 4, left panels).
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps shown in Figure 4.

claim: Positive densities along Lys296 suggest its downward shift (toward the extracellular side), which is detected from 1 μs and becomes most prominent at 4 ms.
source: The positive densities along Lys296 suggest its downward shift (toward the extracellular side), which is detected from 1 μs and becomes most prominent at 4 ms (Figure 4, left panels).
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps.

claim: Positive and negative difference densities around proximal residues in TM7, such as Trp299, indicate an overall downward shift of the middle portion of TM7.
source: In accordance with this shift, positive and negative difference densities are observed around the proximal residues in TM7, such as Trp299, indicating an overall downward shift of the middle portion of TM7.
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps.

claim: The downward shift of TM7 (Helix G) was the most distinct feature in the L-like intermediate of BR.
source: The similar downward shift of TM7 (Helix G) was the most distinct feature in the L-like intermediate of BR, observed in both the cold-trapped synchrotron structure (Neutze et al., 2002) and the recent TR-SFX study (Nango et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to BR structural studies.

claim: In the TR-SFX experiment of BR, the primary retinal isomerization reaction induced local distortion around the C13–C14 double bond of the retinal, which was subsequently propagated as conformational changes to other protein regions, also involving a downward shift of TM7.
source: In the TR-SFX experiment of BR, the primary retinal isomerization reaction induced local distortion around the C13–C14 double bond of the retinal, which was subsequently propagated as conformational changes to other protein regions, also involving a downward shift of TM7.
evidence: This is based on the cited BR TR-SFX study.

claim: At 50 μs, positive and negative difference densities were observed at the putative internal proton acceptor residue, Asp292, indicating a slight downward shift of this residue.
source: Notably, at 50 μs we observed positive and negative difference densities at the putative internal proton acceptor residue, Asp292 (Figure 4, left panels), indicating a slight downward shift of this residue, which might be associated with the proton accepting reaction.
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps at 50 μs.

claim: The downward shift of Asp292 might be associated with the proton accepting reaction.
source: Notably, at 50 μs we observed positive and negative difference densities at the putative internal proton acceptor residue, Asp292 (Figure 4, left panels), indicating a slight downward shift of this residue, which might be associated with the proton accepting reaction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed structural change.

claim: The most prominent change occurs in TM3.
source: The most prominent change occurs in TM3 (Figure 4, right panels).
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps.

claim: A strong negative density appears at Cys167, accompanied by a complementary positive density at the distal site from the retinal, suggesting an outward shift of Cys167.
source: A strong negative density appears at Cys167, accompanied by a complementary positive density at the distal site from the retinal, suggesting an outward shift of Cys167.
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps.

claim: A strong positive density appears near Pro168 on the outside of the TM3 segment, which indicates an outward shift of the cytoplasmic segment of TM3, originating at the helix kink at the Pro168 residue.
source: In addition, a strong positive density appears near Pro168 on the outside of the TM3 segment, which indicates an outward shift of the cytoplasmic segment of TM3, originating at the helix kink at the Pro168 residue.
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps.

claim: Negative and positive densities appear at the C13 methyl group and on the lateral side of the polyene chain of the retinal, respectively.
source: Along with these changes, negative and positive densities appear at the C13 methyl group and on the lateral side of the polyene chain of the retinal, respectively.
evidence: This is directly observed in the difference Fourier maps.

claim: The kink and lateral shift of retinal allows lateral movement of TM6 as well as TM3.
source: This kink and lateral shift of retinal allows lateral movement of TM6 as well as TM3 (Figure 4, right panels).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed structural changes.

claim: The current difference Fourier map is in excellent agreement with the recent MD simulation combined with QM/MM calculations.
source: The current difference Fourier map is in excellent agreement with the recent MD simulation combined with QM/MM calculations (Cheng et al., 2018), in which the retinal adopts a kinked conformation toward TM3 upon the Schiff base deprotonation, probably due to the destabilized resonance structure of the polyene chain (Figure 5), although the QM/MM simulation focuses only on the molecular events after the Schiff base deprotonation and thus does not exactly match the experimental time scale.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to the cited MD/QM/MM simulation.

claim: In the QM/MM simulation, the retinal adopts a kinked conformation toward TM3 upon the Schiff base deprotonation, probably due to the destabilized resonance structure of the polyene chain.
source: The current difference Fourier map is in excellent agreement with the recent MD simulation combined with QM/MM calculations (Cheng et al., 2018), in which the retinal adopts a kinked conformation toward TM3 upon the Schiff base deprotonation, probably due to the destabilized resonance structure of the polyene chain (Figure 5), although the QM/MM simulation focuses only on the molecular events after the Schiff base deprotonation and thus does not exactly match the experimental time scale.
evidence: This is from the cited QM/MM simulation study.

claim: The sequential changes in the difference-Fourier maps suggest that the retinal kink occurs, followed by the consequent outward shift of TM3.
source: Together, the sequential changes in the difference-Fourier maps suggest that the retinal kink occurs, followed by the consequent outward shift of TM3.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-resolved structural data.

claim: The positive/negative peaks at the retinal appear slightly earlier, whereas the change in TM3 becomes slower and reaches the maximum at the later time points of 1 ms and 4 ms.
source: Consistently, the positive/negative peaks at the retinal appear slightly earlier, whereas the change in TM3 becomes slower and reaches the maximum at the later time points of 1 ms and 4 ms (Figure 5).
evidence: This is directly observed from the time-resolved difference maps.

claim: TM7 contributes essentially to the 'central gate', in which Asn297 forms hydrogen bond interactions with Ser102 (TM1) and Glu129 (TM2).
source: TM7 contributes essentially to the 'central gate', in which Asn297 forms hydrogen bond interactions with Ser102 (TM1) and Glu129 (TM2).
evidence: This is based on the dark state structure and established knowledge of the gate structure.

claim: The TM7 shift, as well as the outward shift of Asp292 upon proton acceptance, should lead to rearrangements of the central gate residues.
source: Therefore, the TM7 shift, as well as the outward shift of Asp292 upon proton acceptance, should lead to rearrangements of the central gate residues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed structural changes and the gate structure.

claim: The intracellular end of TM3 shapes the 'inner-gate', in which His173 forms ionic interactions with Arg307 in TM7 and Glu121 and Glu122 in TM2.
source: The intracellular end of TM3 shapes the 'inner-gate', in which His173 forms ionic interactions with Arg307 in TM7 and Glu121 and Glu122 in TM2.
evidence: This is based on the dark state structure and established knowledge of the gate structure.

claim: The recent MD simulation showed a similar retinal kink and subsequent water influx from the intracellular side.
source: The recent MD simulation showed a similar retinal kink and subsequent water influx from the intracellular side (Figure 5; Cheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the MD simulation study.

claim: The conformational change in the middle of TM3 might propagate to the intracellular segment and induce the opening of the inner gate.
source: Therefore, the conformational change in the middle of TM3 might propagate to the intracellular segment and induce the opening of the inner gate.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed TM3 shift and the MD simulation results.

claim: Cys167 and Asp195 have been identified as important residues for channel gating and are thus termed DC-gate or DC-pair, which is conserved among most ChRs.
source: Cys167 and Asp195 have been identified as important residues for channel gating and are thus termed DC-gate or DC-pair, which is conserved among most ChRs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: FTIR and structural studies have suggested that Asp195 functions as the internal proton donor for the deprotonated Schiff base, via an internal hydrated water molecule and Cys167.
source: FTIR and structural studies have suggested that Asp195 functions as the internal proton donor for the deprotonated Schiff base, via an internal hydrated water molecule and Cys167 (Nack et al., 2010; Bamann et al., 2010; Lórenz-Fonfría et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to FTIR and structural studies.

claim: A previous FTIR study showed an increase of the S-H stretching frequency of the Cys167 side chain upon illumination.
source: A previous FTIR study showed an increase of the S-H stretching frequency of the Cys167 side chain upon illumination (Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an FTIR study.

claim: Mutations of the DC-pair residues drastically slowed the open/close kinetics of the channel, resulting in step function opsin (SFO) mutants, with long-lasting photocurrents that can be switched on and off by different wavelengths of light.
source: The DC-pair residues are critical for the fast channel kinetics of ChRs, as mutations of any of them drastically slowed the open/close kinetics of the channel, resulting in step function opsin (SFO) mutants, with long-lasting photocurrents that can be switched on and off by different wavelengths of light (Berndt et al., 2009; Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutational studies.

claim: Previous 2D crystallographic studies of the CrChR2 C128T mutant suggested rearrangements of TM2, 6, and 7 in the open channel conformation.
source: Previous 2D crystallographic studies of the CrChR2 C128T mutant (corresponding to Cys167 in C1C2 [Figure 1—figure supplement 1]) suggested rearrangements of TM2, 6, and 7 in the open channel conformation, that was here induced by the stationary light (Müller et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to 2D crystallographic studies.

claim: The conformational changes observed in the 2D crystallographic studies are partly consistent with the current TR-SFX analysis.
source: These conformational changes are partly consistent with the current TR-SFX analysis.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and previous 2D crystallographic studies.

claim: The TM3 shift is only observed in the current study, indicating the critical role of the Cys residue in the TM3 shift.
source: However, the TM3 shift is only observed in the current study, indicating the critical role of the Cys residue in the TM3 shift.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with the 2D crystallographic studies of the Cys mutant.

claim: The movement of TM7 is similarly observed in both the 2D crystallographic experiments and the current TR-SFX study, although to different degrees.
source: The movement of TM7, on the other hand, is similarly observed in both experiments, although to different degrees.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and previous 2D crystallographic studies.

claim: The conformational changes in TM7 and TM3 are the two important triggers that cooperatively induce channel opening by eliciting sequential conformational changes in the surrounding helices, such as TM2 and TM6.
source: We therefore propose that the conformational changes in TM7 and TM3 are the two important triggers that cooperatively induce channel opening by eliciting sequential conformational changes in the surrounding helices, such as TM2 and TM6 (Figure 6), as observed in the 'open' conformation of the SFO mutant of CrChRs (Müller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed structural changes and comparison to the SFO mutant structure.

claim: This model is in good agreement with the results of the vibrational spectroscopic study showing a two-phasic helix hydration occurring during the early and late stages of the P2 intermediate, in which only the latter leads to the fully-open channel pore.
source: This model is also in good agreement with the results of the vibrational spectroscopic study showing a two-phasic helix hydration occurring during the early and late stages of the P2 intermediate, in which only the latter leads to the fully-open channel pore (Lórenz-Fonfría et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a vibrational spectroscopic study.

claim: Site-directed labeling with infrared sensitive, unnatural amino acids showed that especially hydration changes in the intracellular gate are correlated with channel opening.
source: Furthermore, site-directed labeling with infrared sensitive, unnatural amino acids subsequently showed more specificly, that espacially hydration changes in the intracellular gate are correlated with channel opening (Krause et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a site-directed labeling study.

claim: The TR-SFX experiment revealed two critical conformational changes in TM7 and TM3 that occur during the early part of the photocycle.
source: In summary, our TR-SFX experiment has revealed two critical conformational changes in TM7 and TM3 that occur during the early part of the photocycle, and these triggers would induce water and proton influx and subsequent pore dilation, although only slight structural perturbations in the gate constrictions were observed in the current study, as they were probably affected by the crystal packing interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the TR-SFX data.

claim: These triggers would induce water and proton influx and subsequent pore dilation.
source: In summary, our TR-SFX experiment has revealed two critical conformational changes in TM7 and TM3 that occur during the early part of the photocycle, and these triggers would induce water and proton influx and subsequent pore dilation, although only slight structural perturbations in the gate constrictions were observed in the current study, as they were probably affected by the crystal packing interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed structural changes and comparison to other studies.

claim: Only slight structural perturbations in the gate constrictions were observed in the current study, as they were probably affected by the crystal packing interactions.
source: In summary, our TR-SFX experiment has revealed two critical conformational changes in TM7 and TM3 that occur during the early part of the photocycle, and these triggers would induce water and proton influx and subsequent pore dilation, although only slight structural perturbations in the gate constrictions were observed in the current study, as they were probably affected by the crystal packing interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the data and a speculative explanation for the limited changes.

claim: TM7 is covalently attached to the retinal and thus undergoes a similar shift in other rhodopsin proteins, such as the proton pump BR and the Na+ pump KR2, albeit with some variations.
